extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent applicants, opponents, and IP professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Summarising the EPO Enlarged Board of Appeal decision G 1/23 on whether a marketed product must be reproducible to qualify as prior art under Article 54(2) EPC. The page explains the Board's holdings, reasoning, and practical implications for novelty, inventive step, and IP practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability establishes prior art (Article 54(2) EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: A product becomes prior art when made publicly available; public availability alone is sufficient to establish that a product forms part of the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headnote 1: A product put on the market before the filing date cannot be excluded from the state of the art solely because its composition or internal structure could not be analysed and reproduced by the skilled person. Practical consequence: any commercial release or sale before filing can destroy novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility is not required for prior art status
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproducibility (the ability of the skilled person to manufacture the product anew from starting materials) is not a precondition for treating a marketed product as prior art under Article 54(2) EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EBoA rejected the narrow reading of 'reproduce' as leading to a manifestly absurd result; instead it adopted a broader interpretation so that products available on the market count as prior art even if they cannot realistically be reproduced from scratch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysability influences what technical information is derivable
rubrics_metrics.description: A product's composition and internal features are part of the state of the art to the extent that they can be analysed by the skilled person from the publicly available product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although reproducibility is not required, the Board emphasised that a product's composition is part of the state of the art when the product as such is publicly available and can be analysed by the skilled person. For inventive-step assessment, what matters is the technical teaching realistically derivable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public technical information (brochures, datasheets, publications) counts as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical information about a marketed product that was made publicly available (e.g. brochures, datasheets, scientific publications) before the filing date forms part of the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headnote 2: documentary disclosures accompanying a product are prior art independently of analysability/reproducibility of the physical product itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty criterion focuses on public availability, not motivation to analyse
rubrics_metrics.description: For novelty, it is sufficient that a product was made publicly available; whether the skilled person would be motivated to analyse the product is irrelevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This separates novelty from questions of what technical teaching is realistically derivable, which are more relevant to inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive-step assessment depends on realistic technical teaching derivable
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventive step, what matters is the technical teaching that would realistically be derived by the skilled person from the publicly available product; features that cannot be analysed or reproduced may be disregarded in the inventive-step analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes the inventive-step inquiry highly context-dependent; even if a product is prior art, not all internal features will necessarily be attributable to the skilled person for inventive-step purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product removal or modification does not negate prior art status
rubrics_metrics.description: A product's legal status as prior art is not affected by its later withdrawal from the market or subsequent modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although later disappearance or change may complicate proving particular features in litigation, the abstract technical teaching derivable from the originally marketed product remains permanently part of the state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undue-burden question on analysis left open
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether analysis must be possible without undue burden was not decided in G 1/23 and was left unanswered as moot by the Board in light of the revised framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board acknowledged the issue may arise in future proceedings; practitioners should note that 'analysability without undue burden' could still become relevant in specific cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader interpretation of 'reproducibility' includes mere possession or obtainability
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBoA adopted a broader understanding of 'reproduce' that includes the ability to obtain or possess the marketed product, rather than requiring the skilled person to recreate it from starting materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: many commercially available or natural products cannot realistically be remanufactured, so counting mere market availability as a form of reproducibility avoids a legal fiction detached from commercial/ scientific reality (Reasons 60-62).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical filing and trade-secret implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Because commercialised products are prior art once placed on the market, applicants should file before any public release or sale; selling a product may prevent later patent protection even if the underlying process remains secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice/implication rather than a strict legal test: early filing is critical. Trade-secret strategies may need reconsideration as once a product is sold patent protection may no longer be possible for that product's subject-matter.
